THE RULINGS ON RECORDED CONFLICTS — T-0733.

The final resident audit (T-0512) was the first artifact that could see, in one place, every person the research ledgers had recorded a conflict against. It found them and nothing ruled on any of them. A conflict that is recorded and never adjudicated reads, to anybody downstream, exactly like a conflict nobody found — which is the whole reason this file exists.

WHAT A RULING IS. A written adjudication of a conflict the ledgers already record, made on the evidence already committed. It asserts NOTHING new: every verdict here is a DECLINE, and a decline is what the layer already does silently — the candidate was never asserted, the card carries no identity on its strength. This file writes down the decision that was already taken, names the ground it was taken on, and — the part that was missing — names the record that would REOPEN it. No grade rises here, nobody is minted, no candidate is adopted to close a conflict.

THE RULINGS ARE PINNED TO THE CONFLICT TEXT THEY READ. `ruled_conflicts` carries the conflict strings verbatim as the ledgers state them. If a ledger's conflict is reworded, or a new conflict is added to a person already ruled, the ruling no longer covers that person and the audit's `flag_conflicting_evidence` fires again. That is deliberate: a ruling may never rubber-stamp a conflict it has not read.

THE STANDING CONSTRAINTS ARE NOT CONFLICTS, and folding them in was a defect in the flag. Eight households carry `review_required`, and every one of the eight carries `touches_removal` with it: they are the households the final removal of the Potawatomi from Chicago reaches, and AGENTS.md requires the flag to stand permanently on them so no scene containing them can be marked `released`. It is a standing ethical constraint, not an open evidentiary question, and no research can retire it. The audit now counts them under `flag_standing_constraint` instead.

EVERY PASS, NOT THE NEWEST ONE — T-0845. This file first covered the 68 people the audit could see a conflict on, and the audit could see 68 of 96: `findings()` keeps only the last override written for a person, so a conflict recorded in an early pass and overwritten by a later one stopped being reported and was never ruled. Twenty-eight were in that state. The exporter now reads a person's conflicts from EVERY pass that reviewed them, and refuses a ledger conflict no ruling reaches — the mirror of the orphan-ruling refusal it already made. `cohort_ticket` on those twenty-eight names the pass that WROTE the conflict, which is not always the pass whose outcome the card carries.

verdicts.declined_competing_residence: An independent record documents the candidate living somewhere other than the 1835 town, and nothing puts them under a Chicago roof. The candidate is NOT adopted. This rules out the match on the present record; it does not rule the town person out of existence, and it is not a statement that the two people are different.
verdicts.declined_chronology: The only record joining the candidate to the town stands years away from the scene date, on the wrong side of it. The candidate is NOT adopted. A date gap is not a refutation of identity — it is the absence of a bridge, and a nearer record reopens it.
verdicts.declined_no_bridge: The candidate is plausible on name and period and no record links the two people. The candidate is NOT adopted. Plausibility is not evidence; the town asserts nothing on this candidate's strength.
verdicts.declined_names_not_equated: Two spellings, or two cards, are kept apart rather than collapsed, because no source equates them. The merge is NOT made. Collapsing them would assert an identity no record states, which is the more expensive error here than carrying two rows.
verdicts.declined_forename_refused: The candidate's forename or middle initial is refused by the town's own committed readings. The candidate is NOT adopted. The initial is the discriminator and it disagrees; the printed page that resolves it reopens the question.
verdicts.declined_reading_unverified: The page behind the candidate has not been seen — an index entry, a truncated excerpt, an unavailable scan — so the reading the match rests on cannot be checked. The candidate is NOT adopted. This is a decline on the ACCESS to the evidence, not on the evidence; the page itself reopens it.
verdicts.refused_date_excludes: A date the record itself states makes the identification impossible, not merely unproved: the candidate could not have been the person the Chicago item names. The candidate is REFUSED rather than declined. Every other verdict here says a bridge was not found and names the record that would supply one; this one says no such record can exist, and only a demonstrated error in the stated date reopens it.
verdicts.answered_cards_merged: THE CONFLICT HAS BEEN DECIDED, AND NOT HERE. The record this entry's `reopens_on` asked for arrived, the two cards the ledgers recorded a conflict between are now one card, and the ruling that merged them is in data/residents/card_merge_rulings.json under a named rule. Nothing is adopted by this verdict: it asserts no identity of its own, it names the file and the rule that does, and it exists so that a decline which has stopped being true is retired by a statement rather than by deletion. The conflict text stays pinned verbatim, so a ledger that rewords it un-covers this entry exactly as it would any other.

fraser_wm_h.reopens_on: the merge itself being reopened. T-1133 found that both cards stand on ONE PRINTED LINE — line 55 of the Chicago post office's return of 1 January 1834, read at the page image by T-0424 and tied to both of its readings by T-1010's concordance: the Democrat's impression of 28 January 1834 sets `Wm. H. Fraser`, its impression of 4 March 1834 sets `il. Frazer`. One letter waiting for one man, minted twice. frazer_wm_h is folded onto fraser_wm_h under rule C9, cluster `fraser-frazer`, and kept whole under data/residents/merged/. Pass 11's decline was right on the evidence it had — it looked for an EXTERNAL discriminator and there is none — and the answer came from inside the source both cards were minted from. A second Wm. H. of either spelling read at this town in this window reopens both this and the merge.

scarrett_isaac.moved_note: The card this ruling stood on was folded on 2026-09-15: T-1134 ruled scarritt_isaac and scarrett_isaac one man under C9, on the Chicago Democrat setting the surname three ways for one Isaac — 'Teanc Scarritt' in the list of letters uncalled-for of 28 January 1834, 'Scaredi' and 'Isaac Scarret' on the county's commissioner slate of 6 and 13 August 1834. The ruling MOVES rather than retires, and its verdict is unchanged: what it declined was an OUTSIDE candidate identity, and the fold says nothing about that candidate. NOR IS ITS REOPENING CONDITION MET — it asks for proof of a Chicago HOUSEHOLD at the 1834 postal date, and a candidacy for County Commissioner is a presence in the county's public life and not a roof. The decline stands, on the surviving card.

_retired_doc: A RULING WHOSE CONFLICT HAS BEEN ANSWERED IS RETIRED HERE RATHER THAN DELETED. Every verdict in `rulings` is a DECLINE pinned to a conflict the ledgers state, and its `reopens_on` names the record that would overturn it. When that record arrives and the question is settled somewhere else in the tree, the decline stops being true and may not stand — but the fact that it was made, and the ground it was made on, is part of how the answer was reached. So the entry moves here with the ticket that answered it. tools/export_resident_audit.py refuses a ruling on a person the residents layer no longer holds, which is what made this section necessary: a merge takes the person out from under the ruling.
